q: A table docs has an embedding vector(1536) column. Which query returns the five documents most similar to a query vector :q by cosine distance?
o: SELECT id, title FROM docs ORDER BY embedding <=> :q LIMIT 5
SELECT id, title FROM docs WHERE embedding = :q LIMIT 5
SELECT id, title FROM docs ORDER BY embedding DESC LIMIT 5
SELECT id, title FROM docs GROUP BY embedding LIMIT 5
e: Nearest-neighbor search in pgvector orders by a distance operator and limits the result: <=> is cosine distance, and smaller distances are more similar. Equality would only match identical vectors, and ordering or grouping by the raw vector has no similarity meaning.

q: You want every row whose Euclidean distance to a query vector is less than 6, rather than a fixed top-k. Which query is correct?
o: SELECT * FROM items WHERE embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' < 6
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <=> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 6
SELECT * FROM items WHERE embedding <#> '[3,1,2]' = 6
SELECT * FROM items WHERE vector_dims(embedding) < 6
e: pgvector distance operators return numbers, so you can filter on them; <-> is Euclidean (L2) distance, and the documentation shows exactly this threshold pattern. LIMIT 6 returns six rows regardless of distance, <#> is negative inner product, and vector_dims returns the number of dimensions.

q: Your search returns the 10 nearest products, but only products in the user's chosen category should be returned. How should you write the query in PostgreSQL?
o: Put the filter in the same query: WHERE category = $1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 10
Run the vector search for 10 rows first, then remove other categories in the application
Store the category inside the embedding so the distance already reflects the category
Create a separate database for each category and query only the user's database
e: PostgreSQL lets you combine relational filters with vector ordering in one query, so the database applies the metadata filter as part of retrieval. Filtering after a top-10 search can leave fewer than 10 relevant rows. Embeddings can't encode exact metadata, and a database per category is unnecessary; partial indexes or partitioning can make frequent filters fast.

q: Stored embeddings were generated with text-embedding-3-small. Search quality is poor, and you discover the search API embeds user queries with a different model. What should you do?
o: Embed queries with the same model and dimensions as the stored data
Switch the distance operator from cosine to Euclidean for queries
Increase hnsw.ef_search so more candidates are compared per query
Normalize only the stored vectors so both sides use the same scale
e: Similarity is only meaningful when stored and query vectors come from the same embedding model and dimension space, which is why the semantic search tutorial generates the query embedding the same way as the data embeddings. Changing the operator, search breadth, or normalization doesn't fix vectors from different models.

q: You want a single SQL statement that embeds the user's search text with Azure OpenAI and returns the nearest rows, without an application round trip for the embedding. Which approach works on Azure Database for PostgreSQL?
o: ORDER BY embedding <=> azure_openai.create_embeddings(...)::vector
Call Azure OpenAI from a PL/pgSQL function with an HTTP request through pg_net
Let PgBouncer generate the embedding as the query passes through the pooler
Store the search text and run WHERE content LIKE '%' || :text || '%' instead
e: The azure_ai extension exposes azure_openai.create_embeddings, so a query can embed the input text and order by distance to the stored vectors in one statement, as shown in the semantic search tutorial. PgBouncer only pools connections, and LIKE is keyword matching, not semantic similarity.

q: A cosine distance query returns a distance of 0.18 between two embeddings. What is their cosine similarity?
o: 0.82, because cosine similarity = 1 - cosine distance
0.18, because distance and similarity are the same
5.56, the inverse of the distance
e: pgvector's <=> operator returns cosine distance, which is 1 minus cosine similarity. A distance of 0.18 means a similarity of 0.82; smaller distances mean more similar vectors.

q: Your app already keeps its relational data in Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and you want to add semantic search with the fewest new services. What is the natural choice?
o: Enable pgvector (and optionally pg_diskann) in the existing database
Copy all data into a separate search service before using any embeddings
Store the embeddings in Blob storage and scan them from the application
Use Azure Managed Redis as the system of record for the documents
e: Azure Database for PostgreSQL supports built-in vector search through pgvector, with pg_diskann for scalable ANN indexing, so embeddings can live in the same tables and queries can join and filter on existing data. A separate search service or Blob scans add complexity, and Redis is a cache, not a system of record for documents.

q: To recommend items, you want the centroid (average vector) of all embeddings of items a user liked. Which pgvector feature returns it directly?
o: The AVG(embedding) aggregate
vector_norms(embedding) per row
l2_distance(embedding, embedding)
COUNT(embedding) grouped by user
e: pgvector supports aggregates such as AVG and SUM on vector columns, and they return a vector. vector_norms returns a vector's Euclidean norm, l2_distance returns a number, and COUNT returns the row count.

q: After a model change, some inserts fail and you suspect stored vectors have the wrong number of dimensions. Which function checks a vector's dimension count?
o: vector_dims(embedding)
vector_norms(embedding)
cosine_distance(embedding, embedding)
array_length(embedding)
e: vector_dims returns the number of dimensions of a pgvector value, so you can find rows that don't match the expected size. vector_norms returns the vector's length, and cosine_distance of a vector with itself is 0. array_length works on PostgreSQL arrays, not the vector type.

q: You use pgvector's <#> operator with normalized embeddings. Why does ORDER BY embedding <#> :q (ascending) return the most similar rows first?
o: It returns the negative inner product, so more similar means smaller
It returns cosine similarity, so ascending order puts the best rows first
It returns Euclidean distance, which is the same ranking for any vectors
Ascending order always returns the least similar rows first with any operator
e: pgvector's <#> operator returns the negative inner product, so the most similar vectors have the most negative values and sort first in ascending order. This keeps the ORDER BY ... LIMIT pattern consistent with the other distance operators. <=> is cosine distance and <-> is Euclidean distance.

q: In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app backed by PostgreSQL, what is the database's role when the user asks a question?
o: Retrieve the most relevant chunks, by similarity and filters, for the prompt
Generate the final answer text from the stored chunks with SQL functions
Fine-tune the language model on each question and its retrieved chunks
Store the model weights and run inference close to the data for speed
e: In RAG, the question is embedded, the vector store returns the nearest relevant content, often filtered by metadata such as tenant or category, and that content grounds the model's answer. The database doesn't generate answers, fine-tune models, or host model weights.

q: You want to start using the built-in PgBouncer on an Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. What do you need to do?
o: Turn on pgbouncer.enabled and connect to port 6432 on the same host
Install PgBouncer on a separate VM and point the app at that VM
Create a new server with a different host name that includes PgBouncer
Change the app's connection string to port 5433 on the same host
e: PgBouncer is an optional, built-in feature that you enable per server, after which clients connect to the same host name on port 6432 instead of 5432. No separate VM or server is needed, and 5433 isn't the PgBouncer port.

q: You try to enable the built-in PgBouncer on a Burstable tier server and can't. Which compute tiers support it?
o: General Purpose and Memory Optimized
Burstable only, for small workloads
All tiers, including Burstable
Memory Optimized only, for large servers
e: The PgBouncer documentation states that the built-in PgBouncer is supported on the General Purpose and Memory Optimized compute tiers, in both public and private access networks. To use it, scale the server out of the Burstable tier.

q: Why can the built-in PgBouncer serve up to 10,000 client connections with low overhead?
o: Server connections are used only during a transaction and shared between clients
It caches all query results in memory, so most queries never reach the server
It spreads client connections across several databases on the same server
It closes idle client connections every second to free server resources
e: PgBouncer's lightweight, asynchronous model uses PostgreSQL connections only when needed, inside an open transaction or while a query runs, so many client connections share a small number of server connections. It doesn't cache results or distribute queries across databases.

q: An API opens a new PostgreSQL connection for every HTTP request and closes it afterward. Latency is high because of connection setup. What should you do in the application?
o: Reuse pooled connections with a client pool (psycopg_pool, HikariCP)
Open a new connection twice per request so the second one is warm
Increase work_mem so each new connection is set up faster
Use a smaller embedding model so each request finishes sooner
e: Each new connection pays for TCP, TLS, and authentication, and PostgreSQL starts a backend process for it. Reusing pooled connections removes that overhead, and PgBouncer is especially useful when connection churn is frequent. work_mem and the embedding model don't affect connection setup.

q: After moving to PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode, a feature that relies on session-level state starts behaving unpredictably. Which code is most likely affected?
o: Code that relies on SET variables or temporary tables across transactions
Simple single-statement SELECT queries that run inside one transaction
INSERT statements in autocommit mode that each run as their own transaction
Queries that use bind parameters instead of literal values in the SQL text
e: In transaction pooling, a client gets a server connection only for the length of a transaction, so later transactions may run on a different backend. Session state such as SET values, temporary tables, or session-level advisory locks isn't guaranteed to persist. Stateless statements and parameterized queries work normally.

q: A Python service keeps a pool of PostgreSQL connections and authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID. New connections start failing about an hour after startup. Which Microsoft library is designed to handle this with psycopg?
o: azure-postgresql-auth (token refresh and pooling for psycopg)
azure-storage-blob with a token cache stored in a container
azure-keyvault-secrets to store and rotate the database password
azure-monitor-opentelemetry to detect and reopen failed connections
e: Entra tokens expire (typically after about an hour), so new pooled connections need fresh tokens. The Azure PostgreSQL Auth client library for Python provides Entra ID authentication with automatic token management and connection pooling for psycopg2, psycopg3, and SQLAlchemy. The other libraries serve Blob storage, Key Vault, and telemetry.

q: The same product-detail queries hit Azure Database for PostgreSQL thousands of times per minute, and the data changes rarely. Which architecture reduces database load the most?
o: Cache-aside with Azure Managed Redis, querying PostgreSQL only on misses
Increase max_connections so that the repeated queries run in parallel
Add more IVFFlat lists so that repeated product lookups use the index
Enable strong consistency so that repeated reads are served faster
e: Microsoft's caching guidance for PostgreSQL implements cache-aside with Azure Managed Redis so repeated reads are served from memory and PostgreSQL only handles misses. More connections add load, IVFFlat lists only affect vector indexes, and strong consistency is a Cosmos DB concept.

q: You implement the cache-aside pattern with Azure Managed Redis in front of a database. What happens on a cache miss?
o: The app loads it from the database, stores it in Redis with a TTL, and returns it
Redis loads the item from the database automatically and returns it to the app
The request fails until a background job fills the cache with the missing item
The app writes a placeholder value to Redis and returns an empty response
e: In cache-aside, the application owns the logic: try the cache, and on a miss load from the system of record, store the value in the cache, and return it. Redis doesn't know about your database and doesn't load data on its own.

q: Cached product prices must never be more than 10 minutes out of date, even if an invalidation message is lost. What should you do when writing them to Redis?
o: Set a 10-minute TTL on each key, for example SET key value EX 600
Use the NoEviction policy so cached values stay in memory forever
Store prices without a TTL and refresh the whole cache every week
Use longer key names that include the date the price was cached
e: An expiration bounds how long a stale value can survive, so the next read after it expires reloads fresh data. NoEviction controls what happens when memory is full, not freshness, and keys without a TTL can stay stale indefinitely.

q: When a product is updated in the database, readers must see the new price quickly. Which cache-aside step should the update path perform?
o: Update the database, then delete the product's cache key
Update only the cache and let the database catch up later
Flush the entire cache on every product update
Do nothing; the TTL alone gives immediate consistency
e: Removing the key after updating the system of record forces the next read to fetch the current value, which is the usual cache-aside invalidation step. Writing only to the cache risks losing data, flushing everything causes a stampede of misses, and TTL only bounds staleness rather than removing it immediately.

q: Which authentication method does Microsoft recommend for applications connecting to Azure Managed Redis?
o: Microsoft Entra ID, such as a managed identity
Access keys stored in the app settings
Anonymous access over a private endpoint
A shared password embedded in the image
e: Azure Managed Redis uses Microsoft Entra ID by default for new caches, and Microsoft recommends it over access keys because keys bring password management and security risks. Anonymous access and embedded passwords aren't acceptable for production.

q: A client authenticates to Azure Managed Redis with Microsoft Entra tokens. Connections drop roughly every hour. What does Microsoft recommend?
o: Send a new token at least three minutes before the old one expires
Switch to access keys, which never expire and need no refresh
Disable TLS so that connections can be re-established faster
Restart the cache every hour so all clients reconnect together
e: Entra tokens expire, and the guidance is to send a new token at least three minutes before expiry to avoid connection disruption; Microsoft's client extensions handle this automatically. Access keys are less secure, disabling TLS weakens security, and restarting the cache causes outages.

q: Your team uses a Redis client library that doesn't support the Redis Cluster API, and you need a sharded Azure Managed Redis cache. Which clustering policy should you choose?
o: Enterprise: one endpoint, with a proxy that routes to shards
OSS, because it works with any standard Redis client library
Non-clustered, because it shards data across nodes automatically
Any policy for now, because it can be changed after creation
e: With the Enterprise policy, clients use one endpoint and an internal proxy routes requests to shards, so any standard Redis client works. The OSS policy requires cluster-aware clients but can give lower latency through direct shard connections, and non-clustered isn't sharded. The clustering policy can't be changed after the cache is created.

q: In a cache-aside architecture with Azure Managed Redis and Azure Database for PostgreSQL, which statement about Redis is correct?
o: Redis holds values the app can rebuild from PostgreSQL
Redis is the system of record, and PostgreSQL is the backup
Redis replicates every write back to PostgreSQL automatically
Redis data must never expire, or PostgreSQL gets overloaded
e: In the reference architecture, Managed Redis stores frequently requested values and query results that can be rebuilt from PostgreSQL, which remains the system of record. Redis doesn't write data back to PostgreSQL by itself, and expirations are normal for cached data.

q: A .NET app uses StackExchange.Redis and fails with AuthenticationFailure after a developer pasted an Entra access token into the Password field. What is the recommended approach?
o: Use Microsoft.Azure.StackExchangeRedis with a token credential that refreshes tokens
Paste the access token into the user name field and the object ID as the password
Use the cache's access key permanently and remove Entra authentication from the code
Disable Entra authentication on the cache so that StackExchange.Redis can connect
e: Microsoft provides extension libraries such as Microsoft.Azure.StackExchangeRedis that configure StackExchange.Redis with a token credential, handling user identity, token acquisition, and refresh. Setting a raw token manually goes stale quickly, and falling back to access keys or disabling Entra lowers security.

q: An Azure Managed Redis cache uses the NoEviction policy. What happens when memory is full, and what should you plan for?
o: Writes fail, so plan TTL-based cleanup and capacity alerts
The oldest keys are evicted automatically to make room
The cache scales up automatically to the next SKU
Keys are written to disk until memory is available again
e: With NoEviction, Redis doesn't remove keys to free memory, so memory pressure makes write commands fail. The Well-Architected guidance says to plan explicit cleanup and capacity alerts. Automatic eviction only happens with other policies, and the cache doesn't scale or spill to disk on its own.

q: You want to give a group of 30 developers data access to an Azure Managed Redis cache through Microsoft Entra ID. What limitation applies?
o: Groups aren't supported; add individual users or service principals
Only one Entra user can be added per cache, so share a single account
Entra authentication only works for managed identities, not for people
Groups are supported, but only when access keys are also enabled
e: The Well-Architected guidance for Azure Managed Redis says to add only the required users or service principals because Microsoft Entra groups aren't supported for data-plane access. Many individual users and service principals can be added, and Entra authentication isn't limited to managed identities.

q: You plan to use Azure Managed Redis for vector similarity search. When must you enable the required module?
o: At creation, by enabling RediSearch; it can't be added later
Any time, by running MODULE LOAD from a client connection
After creation, by asking support to install the module
Never; vector search is built into every Managed Redis cache
e: Vector search in Redis requires the RediSearch module, and in Azure Managed Redis modules must be enabled during provisioning; you can't add them afterwards or load them manually. Plan vector search before creating the cache.

q: Which cache configuration does RediSearch require in Azure Managed Redis?
o: The Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy
The OSS clustering policy and the allkeys-lru eviction policy
The non-clustered policy and volatile-ttl eviction
Any clustering policy with any eviction policy
e: RediSearch requires the Enterprise clustering policy and the NoEviction eviction policy, so choosing vector search effectively decides those settings for you. Eviction policies that drop keys would remove indexed documents.

q: Which Azure Managed Redis tier can't use RediSearch for vector search?
o: Flash Optimized
Memory Optimized
Balanced
Compute Optimized
e: RediSearch is supported on the Memory Optimized, Balanced, and Compute Optimized tiers, but not on Flash Optimized.

q: You are creating a Redis vector index. When should you choose HNSW instead of FLAT?
o: For larger datasets, when latency matters more than exact results
When you need exact brute-force results on a small dataset
When vectors are stored as plain strings in hashes
When you want the index to store its keys on disk
e: FLAT is exact brute-force search, suited to smaller datasets or workloads needing exhaustive search, while HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is an approximate nearest neighbor index suited to larger datasets where latency matters more. Data storage format (hash or JSON) doesn't decide the algorithm.

q: Which distance metrics can a Redis vector index use?
o: L2, COSINE, and IP (inner product)
Jaccard, Hamming, and Tanimoto only
Levenshtein and COSINE for text vectors
Manhattan and L2 only, without COSINE
e: Redis vector indexes support L2 (Euclidean), COSINE, and IP (inner product). The right choice depends on the embedding model and whether vectors are normalized.

q: In which Redis data structures can you store vectors for RediSearch, and what else should you store with them?
o: Hashes or JSON, with metadata such as ID, source, and tenant
Only sorted sets, with no metadata stored alongside them
Only lists, with metadata kept in a separate cache
Only streams, with metadata kept in the stream entries
e: Vectors can be stored in hashes or JSON documents, and the guidance is to store metadata alongside each vector, such as document ID, title, source URL, category, timestamp, tenant ID, or access-control fields, so results can be filtered and traced back to sources.

q: A support bot must find similar FAQ entries only within the user's product line and tenant. Which Redis vector search capability should you use?
o: Hybrid queries: TAG or numeric filters combined with KNN
A separate Redis cache for every tenant and product line
Plain GET commands on each FAQ key, filtered in the app
Pub/Sub channels for each product line and tenant
e: RediSearch supports hybrid filtering: metadata filters narrow candidates before or during vector comparison, combined with KNN, range, text, numeric, and tag queries. Separate caches per tenant are costly, GET can't rank by similarity, and Pub/Sub is for messaging.

q: Your chatbot gets many questions that are phrased differently but mean the same thing, and LLM calls are expensive. How can Azure Managed Redis help?
o: As a semantic cache that reuses answers to similar prompts
By caching exact prompt strings, so paraphrases always hit the cache
By storing the language model's weights in memory for faster inference
By replacing the language model with stored answers for every topic
e: Semantic caching stores prompts, embeddings, and completions, and uses vector search to return a cached response when a new prompt is similar enough, reducing LLM cost and latency. Exact-string caching misses paraphrases, and Redis doesn't host or replace the model.

q: Which statement about semantic caching with Azure Managed Redis is correct?
o: It's an app or gateway pattern built on Redis vector search
It's a checkbox on the cache that works without RediSearch
It requires the OSS clustering policy to route prompts
It only works with the Flash Optimized tier of Managed Redis
e: The semantic cache tutorial explains that semantic caching is implemented in the application (for example with RedisVL) or at a gateway such as Azure API Management, while Managed Redis supplies the endpoint and RediSearch vector search. It therefore needs RediSearch, with Enterprise clustering and NoEviction, and Flash Optimized doesn't support RediSearch.

q: You need vector search across caches in two regions with active geo-replication. Which modules can be used together with active geo-replication?
o: RediSearch and RedisJSON
RedisBloom and RedisTimeSeries
All four modules
No modules can be used with geo-replication
e: Only the RediSearch and RedisJSON modules can be used with active geo-replication, which lets you search JSON and vector data across caches synchronized in an active-active configuration. RedisBloom and RedisTimeSeries aren't supported with it.
